title: Affect as Attack
one_line: Can an emotion pushed directly into a language model's hidden state switch off its safety guardrail, even though the prompt looks harmless?

model.why: The proposal's model: strong refusal (84% of HarmBench requests refused), Llama Scope SAEs, the reference model of the refusal-direction literature, runs at about 270 tok/s batched on the M5 Pro. Final choice confirmed by E00 and the model study.

findings.text: In a conversation, the first refusal decides the rest: with four harmful turns in a row the model refuses 90% at turn 4 and 100% at turns 5 to 7.

The paired vectors share one large component (mean cosine 0.79); subtracting it alone gives 33.3%, so it may account for much of the subtraction effect. The paired vectors get 17% of answers flagged as broken (random 1.7%).
The proposal's emotion vectors raise harmful answers no more than random pushes of the same size (20.6% vs 22.1% mean; baseline 14.5%).

A few directions lie above the descriptive random band with few answers flagged as broken: the happiness-specific direction (52.2%) and subtracting loving, anxious, nervous, guilty or grateful (38 to 46%). Twelve seeds cannot make this a calibrated test.
No resolved association between the cosine with the refusal direction and the effect (rho -0.18, p 0.47, wide interval), and projecting the layer-12 refusal candidate out did not lower mean ASR.
Removing one direction (layer 11) takes Llama 3.1 8B from 14.5% to 84.9% harmful answers.
Emotion vectors are real: 81% correct on an independent short-text set (chance 5%).
11 of the proposal's 18 references have wrong metadata and 1 cites the wrong paper; see the Audit page.
